claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae is an opportunistic human pathogen responsible for diseases such as pneumonia, middle ear infections, sepsis, and meningitis.
source: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is an opportunistic human pathogen that is responsible for diseases such as pneumonia, middle ear infections, sepsis, and meningitis (Weiser et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Bogaert et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Weiser et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Bogaert et al., 2004)

claim: S. pneumoniae is listed by the WHO as a priority pathogen for the development of novel antibiotics.
source: S. pneumoniae is listed by the WHO as a priority pathogen for the development of novel antibiotics since it is one of the leading causes of fatal bacterial infections worldwide (Weiser et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Jensen et al., 2015), and antibiotic resistance is on the rise (Càmara et al., 2018; Schrag et al., 2004; Hakenbeck et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Weiser et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Jensen et al., 2015; Càmara et al., 2018; Schrag et al., 2004; Hakenbeck et al., 2012)

claim: S. pneumoniae is one of the leading causes of fatal bacterial infections worldwide.
source: S. pneumoniae is listed by the WHO as a priority pathogen for the development of novel antibiotics since it is one of the leading causes of fatal bacterial infections worldwide (Weiser et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Jensen et al., 2015), and antibiotic resistance is on the rise (Càmara et al., 2018; Schrag et al., 2004; Hakenbeck et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Weiser et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Jensen et al., 2015)

claim: Antibiotic resistance in S. pneumoniae is on the rise.
source: S. pneumoniae is listed by the WHO as a priority pathogen for the development of novel antibiotics since it is one of the leading causes of fatal bacterial infections worldwide (Weiser et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Jensen et al., 2015), and antibiotic resistance is on the rise (Càmara et al., 2018; Schrag et al., 2004; Hakenbeck et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Càmara et al., 2018; Schrag et al., 2004; Hakenbeck et al., 2012)

claim: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines PCV7, PCV10, and PCV13 were developed and rolled out in 2001, 2009, and 2010, respectively.
source: The alarming increase in prevalence of penicillin non-susceptible S. pneumoniae was initially dealt with by the development and roll-out of the pneumococcal conjugate vaccines PCV7, PCV10, and PCV13 in 2001, 2009, and 2010, respectively (Càmara et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Càmara et al., 2018)

claim: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines induce protection against infection caused by 7, 10, or 13 of the most prevalent serotypes of capsular polysaccharides that surround S. pneumoniae.
source: These vaccines induce protection against infection caused by 7, 10, or 13 of the most prevalent serotypes of capsular polysaccharides that surround S. pneumoniae (Bogaert et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bogaert et al., 2004)

claim: Many of the serotypes targeted by pneumococcal conjugate vaccines are associated with penicillin non-susceptibility.
source: Since many of the targeted serotypes are associated with penicillin non-susceptibility, the occurrence of infections with such resistant strains decreased at first (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016; Brueggemann et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016; Brueggemann et al., 2007)

claim: The occurrence of infections with penicillin non-susceptible S. pneumoniae strains decreased initially after vaccine introduction.
source: Since many of the targeted serotypes are associated with penicillin non-susceptibility, the occurrence of infections with such resistant strains decreased at first (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016; Brueggemann et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016; Brueggemann et al., 2007)

claim: S. pneumoniae has high genomic plasticity.
source: However, due to the high genomic plasticity of S. pneumoniae (Hanage et al., 2009; Domenech, 2020), serotype switching created penicillin non-susceptible escape mutants that are not covered by the currently available vaccines and that are once again gaining in prevalence (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hanage et al., 2009; Domenech, 2020)

claim: Serotype switching created penicillin non-susceptible escape mutants not covered by currently available vaccines.
source: However, due to the high genomic plasticity of S. pneumoniae (Hanage et al., 2009; Domenech, 2020), serotype switching created penicillin non-susceptible escape mutants that are not covered by the currently available vaccines and that are once again gaining in prevalence (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016)

claim: Penicillin non-susceptible escape mutants not covered by vaccines are gaining in prevalence.
source: However, due to the high genomic plasticity of S. pneumoniae (Hanage et al., 2009; Domenech, 2020), serotype switching created penicillin non-susceptible escape mutants that are not covered by the currently available vaccines and that are once again gaining in prevalence (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Càmara et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2016)

claim: Penicillin non-susceptible S. pneumoniae strains carry mutations in their penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that decrease their affinity for penicillin.
source: Penicillin non-susceptible S. pneumoniae strains carry a variety of mutations in their penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that decrease their affinity for penicillin and therefore increase resistance (Jensen et al., 2015; Hakenbeck et al., 2012; Chi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Jensen et al., 2015; Hakenbeck et al., 2012; Chi et al., 2007)

claim: PBP mutations that decrease affinity for penicillin also lower susceptibility to other β-lactam antibiotics.
source: These mutations do not only lower the susceptibility to penicillin but also to other β-lactam antibiotics (Prieto et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Prieto et al., 2002)

claim: The efficacy of aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin is usually less affected by PBP mutations than penicillin.
source: However, the efficacy of aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin is usually less affected by these mutations, meaning that amoxicillin remains a viable treatment option for many penicillin non-susceptible strains and therefore became one of the frontline antibiotics to treat pneumococcal infections (Prieto et al., 2002; Baquero et al., 2002; Jacobs, 2004; Bradley et al., 2011; Thiem et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Prieto et al., 2002; Baquero et al., 2002; Jacobs, 2004; Bradley et al., 2011; Thiem et al., 2011)

claim: Amoxicillin became one of the frontline antibiotics to treat pneumococcal infections.
source: However, the efficacy of aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin is usually less affected by these mutations, meaning that amoxicillin remains a viable treatment option for many penicillin non-susceptible strains and therefore became one of the frontline antibiotics to treat pneumococcal infections (Prieto et al., 2002; Baquero et al., 2002; Jacobs, 2004; Bradley et al., 2011; Thiem et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Prieto et al., 2002; Baquero et al., 2002; Jacobs, 2004; Bradley et al., 2011; Thiem et al., 2011)

claim: Highly penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae strains are also amoxicillin non-susceptible.
source: However, highly penicillin-resistant strains have been found to also be amoxicillin non-susceptible (Càmara et al., 2018; Schrag et al., 2004), thereby now also threatening the clinical efficacy of this widely used antibiotic.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Càmara et al., 2018; Schrag et al., 2004)

claim: The authors developed sCRilecs-seq, a high-throughput single-cell based screening approach.
source: To contribute toward this goal, we developed sCRilecs-seq (subsets of CRISPR interference libraries extracted by fluorescence activated cell sorting coupled to next generation sequencing), a high-throughput single-cell based screening approach that we exploited to find targets that could resensitize resistant S. pneumoniae strains toward amoxicillin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript describing a novel method developed by the authors

claim: sCRilecs-seq is based on genome-wide gene silencing using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi).
source: sCRilecs-seq is based upon genome-wide gene silencing using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi), which makes use of a catalytically dead form of the Cas9 enzyme, called dCas9 (Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Qi et al., 2013)

claim: CRISPRi uses a catalytically dead form of the Cas9 enzyme called dCas9.
source: sCRilecs-seq is based upon genome-wide gene silencing using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi), which makes use of a catalytically dead form of the Cas9 enzyme, called dCas9 (Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Qi et al., 2013)

claim: dCas9 is guided toward its target site in the DNA by the provided sgRNA but is unable to introduce double-stranded breaks.
source: dCas9 is guided toward its target site in the DNA by the provided sgRNA(single guide RNA) but is unable to introduce double-stranded breaks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dCas9 function

claim: The dCas9 enzyme acts as a roadblock for RNA polymerase, thereby halting transcription.
source: Instead, the dCas9 enzyme acts as a roadblock for RNA polymerase, thereby halting transcription (Qi et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2016; Bikard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Qi et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2016; Bikard et al., 2013)

claim: CRISPRi gene silencing affects the target gene and influences the expression of an entire transcriptional unit.
source: CRISPRi gene silencing not only affects the target gene but also influences the expression of an entire transcriptional unit (Qi et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2016; Bikard et al., 2013; Liu, 2017; Cui, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Qi et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2016; Bikard et al., 2013; Liu, 2017; Cui, 2018)

claim: CRISPRi technology works at the operon level and generates strong polar effects.
source: This technology therefore works at the operon level and generates strong polar effects that need to be considered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of CRISPRi described in the previous sentences

claim: CRISPRi has been used to perform genome-wide depletion screens in various bacteria.
source: Despite this limitation, CRISPRi has proven to be a very powerful genetic tool to perform genome-wide depletion screens in various bacteria (Cui, 2018; Liu et al., 2021; de Wet et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2019; Rousset et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cui, 2018; Liu et al., 2021; de Wet et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2019; Rousset et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018)

claim: In sCRilecs-seq, subpopulations that display a phenotype of interest are collected using fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS).
source: In the sCRilecs-seq screen used here, subpopulations that display a phenotype of interest are collected using fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS), as has previously been done in eukaryotic cells (Park et al., 2019) and for bacterial transposon libraries (Smith et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Park et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2021)

claim: The abundance of sgRNAs in sorted fractions is compared to a control population to identify genetic factors involved in the phenotype of interest.
source: The abundance of sgRNAs in the sorted fractions is then compared to a defined control population to look for genetic factors involved in the phenotype of interest.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the sCRilecs-seq method

claim: The sCRilecs-seq screen revealed that downregulation of the mevalonate pathway leads to extensive cell elongation.
source: Our screen revealed that downregulation of the mevalonate pathway leads to extensive cell elongation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the sCRilecs-seq screen performed in this study

claim: The mevalonate pathway is the only pathway used by S. pneumoniae to produce isoprenoids.
source: The mevalonate pathway is the only pathway used by S. pneumoniae to produce isoprenoids, a highly diverse class of organic molecules that are essential to all life on earth and that function – among others – in processes such as cell wall synthesis, electron transport, membrane stability, and protein modification (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Heuston et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Heuston et al., 2012)

claim: Isoprenoids are essential to all life on earth and function in processes such as cell wall synthesis, electron transport, membrane stability, and protein modification.
source: The mevalonate pathway is the only pathway used by S. pneumoniae to produce isoprenoids, a highly diverse class of organic molecules that are essential to all life on earth and that function – among others – in processes such as cell wall synthesis, electron transport, membrane stability, and protein modification (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Heuston et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Heuston et al., 2012)

claim: Peptidoglycan synthesis continues even with reduced Und-P levels, but cell constriction is specifically halted.
source: The data suggest that, whereas peptidoglycan synthesis continues even with reduced Und-P levels, cell constriction is specifically halted.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Clomiphene is an FDA-approved drug that inhibits Und-P synthesis.
source: We successfully exploited this knowledge to create a combination treatment strategy where the FDA-approved drug clomiphene, an inhibitor of Und-P synthesis, is paired up with amoxicillin.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by the experimental results showing clomiphene's effects

claim: Clomiphene was shown to block Und-P production in Staphylococcus aureus and to synergize with β-lactam antibiotics.
source: In this combination treatment strategy, amoxicillin is potentiated by the simultaneous administration of clomiphene, a widely used FDA-approved fertility drug that was shown to block Und-P production in Staphylococcus aureus and to synergize with β-lactam antibiotics (Farha et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Farha et al., 2015)

claim: Clomiphene potentiates the antimicrobial activity of amoxicillin against S. pneumoniae.
source: Our results show that clomiphene potentiates the antimicrobial activity of amoxicillin and that combination therapy resensitizes amoxicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Combination therapy with clomiphene and amoxicillin resensitizes amoxicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.
source: Our results show that clomiphene potentiates the antimicrobial activity of amoxicillin and that combination therapy resensitizes amoxicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Amoxicillin-treated S. pneumoniae cells initially elongate before they lyse.
source: As shown in Figure 1A–B and Videos 1–2, amoxicillin-treated cells initially elongate before they lyse.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A-B and Videos 1-2

claim: Amoxicillin causes cell elongation in S. pneumoniae.
source: Indeed, quantitative image analysis confirmed that amoxicillin, like some other β-lactam antibiotics (Tsui et al., 2014), causes cell elongation (Figure 1C), while growth curves in the presence of this antibiotic demonstrate that lysis occurs since optical density (OD) decreases at high amoxicillin concentrations (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative image analysis shown in Figure 1C and citation (Tsui et al., 2014)

claim: Lysis occurs at high amoxicillin concentrations as demonstrated by decreasing optical density.
source: Indeed, quantitative image analysis confirmed that amoxicillin, like some other β-lactam antibiotics (Tsui et al., 2014), causes cell elongation (Figure 1C), while growth curves in the presence of this antibiotic demonstrate that lysis occurs since optical density (OD) decreases at high amoxicillin concentrations (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Ciprofloxacin did not induce cell elongation in S. pneumoniae.
source: As expected, ciprofloxacin did not induce cell elongation (Sorg and Veening, 2015; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citation (Sorg and Veening, 2015)

claim: Synergy between antimicrobial compounds is most often detected when they target the same process.
source: Because it was shown that synergy between antimicrobial compounds is most often detected when they target the same process (Brochado et al., 2018), we hypothesized that targets whose inhibition would cause cell elongation, like amoxicillin, could potentially reinforce the antibacterial effect of this antibiotic.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Brochado et al., 2018)

claim: The sCRilecs-seq screen identified 70 sgRNAs that were significantly enriched in the fraction of the population with the highest FSC values.
source: Following this strategy, we were able to identify 70 sgRNAs that were significantly enriched in the fraction of the population with the highest FSC values (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the sCRilecs-seq screen, supported by data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary materials

claim: All eight selected sgRNAs validated from the sCRilecs-seq screen led to increased FSC values and larger cell sizes upon depletion.
source: These results demonstrate that all selected hits from the sCRilecs-seq screen led to increased FSC values and larger cell sizes upon depletion, meaning that all sgRNAs selected for validation represent true positive hits.
evidence: Supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 2C-D

claim: Many of the significant hits from the sCRilecs-seq screen are known to be involved in processes that influence cell size and/or morphology.
source: The reliability of our screening approach is also reflected by the fact that many of the significant hits are known to be involved in processes that influence cell size and/or morphology (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of screen results with published literature

claim: The sCRilecs-seq screen detected late cell division proteins DivIB, DivIC, FtsL, and FtsW as hits.
source: Such known regulators that are picked up by our screen include the late cell division proteins DivIB, DivIC, FtsL, and FtsW (Massidda et al., 2013) and the cell cycle regulator GpsB (Rued et al., 2017; Land et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Massidda et al., 2013)

claim: The sCRilecs-seq screen detected the cell cycle regulator GpsB as a hit.
source: Such known regulators that are picked up by our screen include the late cell division proteins DivIB, DivIC, FtsL, and FtsW (Massidda et al., 2013) and the cell cycle regulator GpsB (Rued et al., 2017; Land et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Rued et al., 2017; Land et al., 2013)

claim: GO enrichment analysis detected 'regulation of cell shape' as an enriched biological process category.
source: Biological processes found to be enriched include 'regulation of cell shape' (fold change 8.43, p value 1.03E-05), 'cell wall organization' (fold change 6.71, p value 7.24E-04), 'cell division' (fold change 6.63, p value 1.24E-04), and 'peptidoglycan biosynthetic process' (fold change 6.27, p value 2.26E-03).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis of the screen hits

claim: GO enrichment analysis detected 'cell wall organization' as an enriched biological process category.
source: Biological processes found to be enriched include 'regulation of cell shape' (fold change 8.43, p value 1.03E-05), 'cell wall organization' (fold change 6.71, p value 7.24E-04), 'cell division' (fold change 6.63, p value 1.24E-04), and 'peptidoglycan biosynthetic process' (fold change 6.27, p value 2.26E-03).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis of the screen hits

claim: GO enrichment analysis detected 'cell division' as an enriched biological process category.
source: Biological processes found to be enriched include 'regulation of cell shape' (fold change 8.43, p value 1.03E-05), 'cell wall organization' (fold change 6.71, p value 7.24E-04), 'cell division' (fold change 6.63, p value 1.24E-04), and 'peptidoglycan biosynthetic process' (fold change 6.27, p value 2.26E-03).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis of the screen hits

claim: GO enrichment analysis detected 'peptidoglycan biosynthetic process' as an enriched biological process category.
source: Biological processes found to be enriched include 'regulation of cell shape' (fold change 8.43, p value 1.03E-05), 'cell wall organization' (fold change 6.71, p value 7.24E-04), 'cell division' (fold change 6.63, p value 1.24E-04), and 'peptidoglycan biosynthetic process' (fold change 6.27, p value 2.26E-03).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis of the screen hits

claim: Many hits from the sCRilecs-seq screen target the production of teichoic acids.
source: Besides these processes, it is also notable that many hits target the production of teichoic acids.
evidence: This is an observation from the screen results

claim: Teichoic acids are an important component of the S. pneumoniae cell envelope and are necessary to maintain proper cell morphology.
source: These glycopolymers are an important component of the S. pneumoniae cell envelope and are indeed necessary to maintain proper cell morphology (Liu, 2017; Vollmer et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Liu, 2017; Vollmer et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2013)

claim: The sCRilecs-seq screen identified several components of the Sec translocase system as hits.
source: Our list of hits also contains several components of the Sec translocase system, thereby confirming the previously published link between this translocase and S. pneumoniae cell division (Tsui et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Tsui et al., 2011)

claim: The VicRK two-component system is thought to control cell size by regulating the expression of the murine hydrolase PcsB.
source: Additional hits include the operon encoding the VicRK two-component system that is thought to control cell size by regulating the expression of the murine hydrolase PcsB that is also detected as a significant hit in our screen and depletion of which is known to lead to uncontrolled peptidoglycan synthesis and large cells (Ng et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ng et al., 2004)

claim: Depletion of PcsB leads to uncontrolled peptidoglycan synthesis and large cells.
source: Additional hits include the operon encoding the VicRK two-component system that is thought to control cell size by regulating the expression of the murine hydrolase PcsB that is also detected as a significant hit in our screen and depletion of which is known to lead to uncontrolled peptidoglycan synthesis and large cells (Ng et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ng et al., 2004)

claim: The most highly upregulated GO category was 'isoprenoid biosynthetic process'.
source: Finally, whereas the GO enrichment analysis rendered a lot of expected and anticipated results, the most highly upregulated category was 'isoprenoid biosynthetic process' (fold change 13.43, p value 6.45E-03).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis of the screen hits

claim: S. pneumoniae synthesizes isoprenoids through the mevalonate pathway.
source: S. pneumoniae synthesizes isoprenoids through the mevalonate pathway (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Wilding et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Wilding et al., 2000)

claim: The mevalonate pathway produces the C5 precursors isopentenyl diphosphate and dimethylallyl diphosphate.
source: This pathway, with mevalonic acid (mevalonate) as intermediate, produces the C5 precursors, isopentenyl diphosphate, and dimethylallyl diphosphate (Figure 3A), which can be condensed into large and diverse isoprenoids (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015) and shown in Figure 3A

claim: All proteins involved in the mevalonate pathway in S. pneumoniae are encoded by two different operons.
source: In S. pneumoniae, all proteins involved in the mevalonate pathway are encoded by two different operons (Wilding et al., 2000; Slager et al., 2018), both of which were identified as hits in our sCRilecs-seq screen.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Wilding et al., 2000; Slager et al., 2018)

claim: Both mevalonate operons were identified as hits in the sCRilecs-seq screen.
source: In S. pneumoniae, all proteins involved in the mevalonate pathway are encoded by two different operons (Wilding et al., 2000; Slager et al., 2018), both of which were identified as hits in our sCRilecs-seq screen.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the sCRilecs-seq screen

claim: Depletion of mevalonate operons led to a very large increase in cell length.
source: Phase contrast microscopy of cells depleted for the mevalonate pathway operons demonstrated large increases in cell length (Figure 3C–D), confirming the sCRilecs-seq screen.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C-D

claim: Cells on average attained more than twice their normal length when the mevalonate operons were depleted.
source: Cells on average attained more than twice their normal length when the mevalonate operons were depleted (Figure 3D), whereas the mean cell width increased 1.35× for depletion of operon 1 and 1.25× for operon 2.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Depletion of the mevalonate operons led to severe growth defects.
source: In addition to cell elongation, depletion of the mevalonate operons led to severe growth defects (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The elongated phenotype and growth defects caused by mevalonate operon depletion could be complemented by ectopic induction of the mevalonate operons with IPTG.
source: Importantly, the elongated phenotype and observed growth defects could be complemented by ectopic induction of the mevalonate operons with an optimized concentration of IPTG (Figure 3F–G), demonstrating that these phenotypes are not due to polar effects of the mutations.
evidence: Supported by complementation data shown in Figure 3F-G

claim: Time-lapse microscopy showed that cells initially continue to grow and elongate before lysis takes place upon mevalonate operon depletion.
source: Time-lapse microscopy upon depletion of the mevalonate operons confirmed these findings, showing that cells initially continue to grow and elongate before lysis takes place (Figure 3J and Videos 2–3).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3J and Videos 2-3

claim: Lysis upon mevalonate operon depletion was found to be partially dependent on LytA.
source: Of note, lysis was found to be partially dependent on LytA, and phenotypes were reproducible in deletion/complementation strains that do not carry the hlpA-gfp and ftsZ-mCherry fusions (VL3708 and VL3709) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-G

claim: The mevalonate pathway is essential for S. pneumoniae viability.
source: These results confirm that the mevalonate pathway is essential for S. pneumoniae viability and that it is the only pathway through which this bacterium can synthesize isoprenoids (Wilding et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing inability to delete mevalonate operons without supplementation, and citation (Wilding et al., 2000)

claim: Mevalonate operon 1 can be deleted when mevalonic acid is added to the growth medium.
source: However, when mevalonic acid – an intermediary in the mevalonate pathway (Figure 3A) – was added to the growth medium, we were able to delete operon 1, as was also shown previously in S. pneumoniae and S. aureus (Wilding et al., 2000; Balibar et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2013; Reichert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations (Wilding et al., 2000; Balibar et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2013; Reichert et al., 2018)

claim: Deleting mevalonate operon 2 remained impossible even with mevalonic acid supplementation.
source: As expected, based on pathway architecture, deleting operon 2 – which encodes proteins that work downstream of mevalonic acid – remained impossible.
evidence: This is an experimental result that is consistent with the pathway architecture

claim: Decreasing the concentration of mevalonic acid led to cell elongation and growth defects in the Δoperon 1 strain.
source: However, decreasing the concentration of mevalonic acid led to cell elongation and growth defects that became more pronounced at lower concentrations, thereby phenocopying genetic depletion of operon 1 and 2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H-I

claim: When no mevalonic acid is provided, cultures of the Δoperon 1 strain are driven to full extinction.
source: In fact, when no mevalonic acid is provided at all, cultures are driven to full extinction (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Mevalonate depleted cells contain many unconstricted FtsZ rings.
source: Microscopic investigation of mevalonate depleted cells showed that these bacteria contain many unconstricted FtsZ rings (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-B

claim: Depletion of the mevalonate operons resulted in an unusually high occurrence of initiated septa that appear to be blocked for further constriction.
source: High-resolution investigation of this phenotype by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) showed that depletion of the mevalonate operons resulted in an unusually high occurrence of initiated septa that appear to be blocked for further constriction, whereas division septa at all stages of constriction could be found in a wild-type (wt) strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Depletion of mevalonate operons eliminated septal peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Quantitative image analysis of sites of active peptidoglycan synthesis labeled with FDAAs shows that depletion of mevalonate operons eliminated septal peptidoglycan synthesis since virtually no narrow sBADA or RADA bands can be found (E) and that the intensity of FDAA labeling decreased upon mevalonate depletion, indicating that peripheral peptidoglycan synthesis was slowed down (F).
evidence: Supported by FDAA labeling data shown in Figure 4E-F

claim: The intensity of FDAA labeling decreased upon mevalonate depletion, indicating that peripheral peptidoglycan synthesis was slowed down.
source: Quantitative image analysis of sites of active peptidoglycan synthesis labeled with FDAAs shows that depletion of mevalonate operons eliminated septal peptidoglycan synthesis since virtually no narrow sBADA or RADA bands can be found (E) and that the intensity of FDAA labeling decreased upon mevalonate depletion, indicating that peripheral peptidoglycan synthesis was slowed down (F).
evidence: Supported by FDAA labeling data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Mevalonate depletion leads to filamentation because constriction and cell division are blocked while peptidoglycan synthesis that contributes to cell elongation can still occur.
source: Taken together, these results strongly indicate that mevalonate depletion leads to filamentation because constriction and cell division are blocked while peptidoglycan synthesis that contributes to cell elongation can still occur, albeit at a lower rate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in Figure 4

claim: Extended depletion of mevalonate operons eventually affects the integrity and/or rigidity of the peptidoglycan mesh, leading to cell lysis.
source: Since lysis usually occurs through weakening of the peptidoglycan cell wall (Yao et al., 2012), we hypothesize that extended depletion of mevalonate operons eventually affects the integrity and/or rigidity of the peptidoglycan mesh, leading to cell lysis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of lysis and citation (Yao et al., 2012)

claim: The primary effect of mevalonate depletion is a block in constriction necessary for cell division.
source: However, considering the initial phenotypes found, we conclude that the primary effect of mevalonate depletion is a block in constriction necessary for cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented

claim: A shortage in the production of Und-P is responsible for the phenotypic effects of perturbed mevalonate production.
source: However, given the nature of the observed phenotype, we thought it most likely that a shortage in the production of Und-P would be responsible for the observed effects.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is subsequently tested experimentally

claim: UppP, the gene product that dephosphorylates undecaprenyl pyrophosphate (Und-PP) to create Und-P, was found as a hit in the sCRilecs-seq screen.
source: This hypothesis is also supported by the fact that UppP, the gene product that dephosphorylates undecaprenyl pyrophosphate (Und-PP) to create Und-P, is found as a hit that increases cell size in our sCRilecs-seq screen (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the sCRilecs-seq screen

claim: Und-PP is synthesized by UppS by the addition of eight isopentenyl units to the C15 isoprenoid farnesyl-PP.
source: Und-P is produced by the dephosphorylation of Und-PP, which is in turn synthesized by UppS (undecaprenyl pyrophosphate synthase) by the addition of eight isopentenyl units to the C15 isoprenoid farnesyl-PP (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Bouhss et al., 2008; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Boronat and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2015; Bouhss et al., 2008) and shown in Figure 5A

claim: When the uppS deletion/complementation strain was grown in absence of uppS expression, cells were elongated and growth was reduced.
source: When this strain was grown in absence of uppS expression, cells were elongated and growth was reduced (Figure 5C–D), thereby phenocopying mevalonate mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: UppS depleted cells contained multiple unconstricted Z-rings and initiated septa that failed to constrict further.
source: In addition, UppS depleted cells contained multiple unconstricted Z-rings and initiated septa that failed to constrict further, even though peptidoglycan synthesis still occurred as demonstrated by TEM and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5D-F

claim: The negative effects caused by depletion of the mevalonate operons can be explained by insufficient production of Und-PP and subsequently Und-P.
source: We thus conclude that the negative effects caused by depletion of the mevalonate operons can be explained by insufficient production of Und-PP and subsequently Und-P.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that UppS depletion phenocopies mevalonate depletion

claim: Deletion of the cps operon responsible for capsule synthesis did not result in cell elongation or affect growth rate.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B, cps mutant cells were not elongated nor was growth rate affected, as also shown before (Barendt et al., 2009), demonstrating that a shortage of capsule synthesis does not contribute to the mevalonate depletion phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B and citation (Barendt et al., 2009)

claim: MraY couples the MurNAc-pentapeptide moiety to Und-P for peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: For peptidoglycan, it is known that the MurNAc-pentapeptide moiety that is produced in the cytoplasm is coupled to Und-P by MraY (Bouhss et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bouhss et al., 2008)

claim: SPV_1620 is the enzyme that couples teichoic acid precursors to Und-P in S. pneumoniae.
source: Based on sequence similarity, bioinformatic analysis indicated that the enzyme that does the same for teichoic acid precursors in S. pneumoniae is SPV_1620 (Denapaite et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Denapaite et al., 2012)

claim: Depletion of MraY was highly similar to the mevalonate phenotype at early time points.
source: Depletion of MraY, on the other hand, was highly similar to the mevalonate phenotype at early time points.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-H

claim: A deficiency in peptidoglycan precursors at the site of cell wall synthesis is mainly responsible for the elongated phenotype observed when components of the mevalonate pathway are depleted.
source: We thus conclude that a deficiency in peptidoglycan precursors at the site of cell wall synthesis is mainly responsible for the elongated phenotype that is observed when components of the mevalonate pathway are depleted.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing MraY and SPV_1620 depletion

claim: A certain threshold level of peptidoglycan precursors is needed for cells to divide, while cell elongation can proceed with a lower amount of peptidoglycan precursors.
source: Since we previously showed that this elongated phenotype is caused by continued peptidoglycan synthesis in the absence of cell constriction, it appears as though a certain threshold level of peptidoglycan precursors is needed for cells to divide. Cell elongation, on the other hand, can proceed with a lower amount of peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented

claim: GO enrichment analysis of the second sCRilecs-seq screen identified cell division and closely related GO categories as significantly overrepresented in elongated cells.
source: GO enrichment analysis identified cell division and closely related GO categories as significantly overrepresented in elongated cells (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis of the second screen

claim: Depleting genes involved in cell division leads to additional cell elongation upon mevalonate depletion.
source: This suggests that depleting genes involved in cell division (such as significant hits ftsZ, divIB, divIC, and ftsW) will lead to additional cell elongation upon mevalonate depletion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GO enrichment analysis results

claim: sgRNAs enriched in the small fraction of the population are often involved in protein expression or energy metabolism.
source: On the other hand, sgRNAs that are enriched in the small fraction of the population are often involved in protein expression (RNA biosynthesis, translation, tRNA aminoacylation, etc.) or energy metabolism (glycolysis, ATP synthesis coupled proton transport, etc.).
evidence: This is an observation from the second sCRilecs-seq screen results

claim: Halting or interfering with protein expression or energy production reduces cell elongation caused by mevalonate deficiency.
source: Halting or interfering with protein expression or energy production therefore appears to reduce cell elongation caused by mevalonate deficiency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the second sCRilecs-seq screen results

claim: The sgRNA targeting divIVA was strongly depleted from the fraction of the population with the largest cell sizes and highly enriched in the fraction with the smallest cells.
source: For example, the sgRNA targeting divIVA was strongly depleted from the fraction of the population with the largest cell sizes and also highly enriched in the fraction with the smallest cells, indicating that the depletion of DivIVA hampers cell elongation upon mevalonate depletion.
evidence: This is a finding from the second sCRilecs-seq screen

claim: DivIVA activity is necessary for cell elongation.
source: DivIVA activity was previously shown to be necessary for cell elongation, and DivIVA is known to be phosphorylated by the serine/threonine kinase StkP that is thought to constitute a molecular switch that governs elongation and division (Vollmer et al., 2019; Fleurie et al., 2014; Beilharz et al., 2012; Fleurie et al., 2012; Nováková et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Vollmer et al., 2019; Fleurie et al., 2014; Beilharz et al., 2012; Fleurie et al., 2012; Nováková et al., 2010)

claim: A double depletion of the first mevalonate operon and DivIVA leads to reduced cell lengths compared to depletion of mevalonate alone.
source: Indeed, we confirmed that a double depletion of the first mevalonate operon and DivIVA leads to reduced cell lengths in comparison to the depletion of mevalonate alone (Figure 5J), indicating that also upon mevalonate depletion DivIVA activity assists cell elongation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J

claim: Elongation enforced by mevalonate depletion is not fully dependent on DivIVA activity.
source: However, cells depleted for both mevalonate and DivIVA are still larger than wt cells, indicating that a limited amount of elongation still occurs. Elongation enforced by mevalonate depletion is therefore not fully dependent on DivIVA activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 5J

claim: FtsW and RodA are thought to be the primary transglycosylases responsible for peptidoglycan polymerization during cell division and cell elongation, respectively.
source: These proteins are thought to be the primary transglycosylases responsible for peptidoglycan polymerization during cell division and cell elongation, respectively (Cho et al., 2016; Meeske et al., 2016; Taguchi et al., 2019; Tsui et al., 2016; Perez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cho et al., 2016; Meeske et al., 2016; Taguchi et al., 2019; Tsui et al., 2016; Perez et al., 2019)

claim: Pbp2b is the transpeptidase that works in conjunction with RodA to perform peripheral peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Moreover, CRISPRi depletion of Pbp2b, the transpeptidase that works in conjunction with RodA to perform peripheral peptidoglycan synthesis (Vollmer et al., 2019; Berg et al., 2013; Tsui et al., 2016), showed up in the short-cell fraction (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Vollmer et al., 2019; Berg et al., 2013; Tsui et al., 2016)

claim: RodA together with Pbp2b is at least partly responsible for cell elongation that occurs upon mevalonate depletion.
source: These results indicate that RodA together with Pbp2b is at least partly responsible for cell elongation that occurs upon mevalonate depletion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the second sCRilecs-seq screen results

claim: Pbp2x is the transpeptidase that is essential for septal peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Because Pbp2x, the transpeptidase that is essential for septal peptidoglycan synthesis (Tsui et al., 2014; Massidda et al., 2013), is encoded in an operon together with mraY, its effect on mevalonate-dependent cell elongation could not be directly assessed in the sCRilecs-seq screen.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Tsui et al., 2014; Massidda et al., 2013)

claim: Depletion of Pbp2x led to an increase in cell length, and this phenotype was augmented under low mevalonate levels.
source: As shown in Figure 5J, depletion of Pbp2x indeed led to an increase in cell length, as reported before (Tsui et al., 2014), and this phenotype was augmented under low mevalonate levels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and citation (Tsui et al., 2014)

claim: Elongation upon mevalonate depletion was less pronounced when pbp2x was simultaneously repressed.
source: However, elongation upon mevalonate depletion was less pronounced when pbp2x was simultaneously repressed, hinting at a role for this septation-specific PBP in elongation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J

claim: The antibacterial effect of amoxicillin is increased upon mevalonate depletion.
source: In a first step, we confirmed that the antibacterial effect of amoxicillin – but not that of the fluoroquinolone ciprofloxacin – is increased upon mevalonate depletion, since amoxicillin could inhibit growth already at sub-MIC concentrations when mevalonate became limiting (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: The antibacterial effect of ciprofloxacin is not increased upon mevalonate depletion.
source: In a first step, we confirmed that the antibacterial effect of amoxicillin – but not that of the fluoroquinolone ciprofloxacin – is increased upon mevalonate depletion, since amoxicillin could inhibit growth already at sub-MIC concentrations when mevalonate became limiting (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: Simvastatin and farnesol are expected to block the HMG-CoA reductase MvaA.
source: Three compounds were selected; simvastatin and farnesol are expected to block the HMG-CoA reductase MvaA that catalyzes one of the first steps of the mevalonate pathway (Masadeh et al., 2012; Bergman et al., 2011; Kaneko et al., 2011), while clomiphene was shown to inhibit UppS in S. aureus and is counteracted by the addition of exogenous Und-P33.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Masadeh et al., 2012; Bergman et al., 2011; Kaneko et al., 2011)

claim: Simvastatin and farnesol were not able to cause cell elongation in S. pneumoniae.
source: Unfortunately, simvastatin and farnesol were not able to cause cell elongation.
evidence: This is an experimental result from testing these compounds

claim: Simvastatin is a specific inhibitor of eukaryotic-type HMG-CoA reductase and is expected to be far less active against the bacterial counterpart.
source: Simvastatin on the other hand is a specific inhibitor of eukaryotic-type HMG-CoA reductase and is expected to be far less active against the bacterial counterpart of this enzyme (Perez and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Perez and Rodríguez-Concepción, 2013)

claim: The addition of clomiphene resulted in filamentation in S. pneumoniae.
source: However, the addition of clomiphene did result in filamentation under our conditions (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Time-lapse analysis showed considerable cell elongation in the presence of clomiphene.
source: Indeed, time-lapse analysis showed considerable cell elongation in the presence of clomiphene, albeit less than upon depletion of the mevalonate operons potentially due to the lag in severe and lethal effects upon gradual genetic depletion (Figure 6B and Video 5).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and Video 5

claim: Sub-MIC concentrations of clomiphene led to severe growth defects in cultures that were slightly depleted for mevalonate.
source: Additionally, clomiphene most likely targets the production of Und-P, since sub-MIC concentrations of clomiphene led to severe growth defects in cultures that were slightly depleted for mevalonate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Clomiphene did not affect the efficacy of ciprofloxacin.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6C, clomiphene did not affect the efficacy of ciprofloxacin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Clomiphene potentiated the antimicrobial activity of amoxicillin.
source: However, for amoxicillin, potentiation by clomiphene was observed (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: In the presence of clomiphene, the concentration of amoxicillin necessary to block pneumococcal growth decreased by a factor 2–8.
source: Indeed, in the presence of clomiphene, the concentration of amoxicillin necessary to block pneumococcal growth decreased by a factor 2–8 (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Table 1

claim: Clomiphene potentiated the antimicrobial activity of amoxicillin against clinical resistant strains.
source: Results are presented in Figure 6F–H and Table 1 and show that clomiphene potentiated the antimicrobial activity of amoxicillin also against clinical resistant strains.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F-H and Table 1

claim: The potentiation of amoxicillin by clomiphene was considerably stronger in resistant genetic backgrounds.
source: Moreover, the potentiation was considerably stronger in these resistant genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the potentiation effects in different strains

claim: The concentration of amoxicillin necessary to block growth of resistant strains decreased by a factor 16–64 in the presence of 8 µg/ml of clomiphene.
source: Indeed, the concentration of amoxicillin necessary to block growth of these resistant strains decreased by a factor 16–64 in the presence of 8 µg/ml of clomiphene (Table 1), thereby reducing resistance below the EUCAST clinical breakpoint for sensitivity (0.5 µg/ml) (EUCAST, 2021).
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Table 1 and citation (EUCAST, 2021)

claim: The combination treatment strategy can resensitize amoxicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae strains below the EUCAST clinical breakpoint for sensitivity in vitro.
source: Our rationally designed combination treatment strategy can thus resensitize amoxicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae strains so that they once again become fully susceptible to amoxicillin in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MIC data showing reduction below the clinical breakpoint

claim: Treatment with amoxicillin alone significantly lowered bacterial counts in the murine pneumonia model.
source: Whereas treatment with amoxicillin alone significantly lowered bacterial counts, administering only clomiphene did not influence the bacterial load (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: Administering only clomiphene did not influence the bacterial load in the murine pneumonia model.
source: Whereas treatment with amoxicillin alone significantly lowered bacterial counts, administering only clomiphene did not influence the bacterial load (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: Treating mice with both clomiphene and amoxicillin did not show a stronger effect than treatment with amoxicillin alone.
source: Treating mice with both clomiphene and amoxicillin did not show a stronger effect than treatment with amoxicillin alone, meaning that the potentiation of amoxicillin we observed in vitro could not be detected in vivo (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: The active concentration of clomiphene in the lung was lower than 4 µg/ml.
source: This experiment indicated that the active concentration of clomiphene in the lung was lower than 4 µg/ml, which could explain the absence of amoxicillin potentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: Resistance toward β-lactam antibiotics in S. pneumoniae is mostly caused by mosaic PBPs formed by recombination events following horizontal gene transfer.
source: In S. pneumoniae, resistance toward β-lactam antibiotics is mostly caused by mosaic PBPs. These resistance-conferring mosaic PBPs are formed by recombination events following horizontal gene transfer from β-lactam resistant donor strains (Jensen et al., 2015; Hakenbeck et al., 2012; Gibson et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Jensen et al., 2015; Hakenbeck et al., 2012; Gibson et al., 2021)

claim: Many resistance-conferring PBP mutations are associated with considerable fitness costs that need to be compensated for.
source: It has been shown that many resistance-conferring PBP mutations are associated with considerable fitness costs that need to be compensated for (Albarracín Orio et al., 2011; Zerfass et al., 2009; Smith and Klugman, 2001) and that mosaic PBPs significantly alter the cell wall structure, potentially by a decrease in affinity for their natural substrate (Garcia-Bustos and Tomasz, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Albarracín Orio et al., 2011; Zerfass et al., 2009; Smith and Klugman, 2001)

claim: Mosaic PBPs significantly alter the cell wall structure, potentially by a decrease in affinity for their natural substrate.
source: It has been shown that many resistance-conferring PBP mutations are associated with considerable fitness costs that need to be compensated for (Albarracín Orio et al., 2011; Zerfass et al., 2009; Smith and Klugman, 2001) and that mosaic PBPs significantly alter the cell wall structure, potentially by a decrease in affinity for their natural substrate (Garcia-Bustos and Tomasz, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Garcia-Bustos and Tomasz, 1990)

claim: Mosaic PBPs display suboptimal activity which allows them to remain active during amoxicillin treatment but fail when peptidoglycan precursors become limiting.
source: We therefore speculate that these mosaic PBPs display suboptimal activity which allows them to remain active during amoxicillin treatment but fail to carry out their task if the amount of peptidoglycan precursors available to them becomes limiting due to a deficiency in Und-P production.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed stronger potentiation in resistant strains

claim: Suboptimal, resistance-conferring, mosaic PBPs are the reason why clomiphene has a much stronger potentiation effect in resistant strains.
source: We believe that these suboptimal, resistance-conferring, mosaic PBPs are the reason why clomiphene has a much stronger potentiation effect in these strains than in all other tested strains and species.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations

claim: Clomiphene is an FDA-approved prodrug administered as a racemic mixture of two stereoisomers.
source: Clomiphene is an FDA-approved prodrug that is administered as a racemic mixture of two stereoisomers and is metabolized by the liver into active compounds that stimulate ovulation in anovulatory women (Dickey and Holtkamp, 1996; Huppert, 1979; Nasseri and Ledger, 2001; Mürdter et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Dickey and Holtkamp, 1996; Huppert, 1979; Nasseri and Ledger, 2001; Mürdter et al., 2012)

claim: One or both of the clomiphene prodrug isomers exert the antibacterial effect.
source: However, since we observe antibacterial effects and amoxicillin potentiation in vitro, it seems likely that one or both of the prodrug isomers exert the desired effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of antibacterial effects in vitro
